newsitem.title: JAPAN: Peru-bashing breaks out in small Japan town.
newsitem.headline: Peru-bashing breaks out in small Japan town.

text.p: Shops and cars owned by Peruvians in this immigrant community have been stoned in an outbreak of Peru-bashing by xenophobic Japanese, residents said on Tuesday.

"I fear this is setting off a kind of mood of bullying or discrimination against us by Japanese," said Kiyoshi Machida, a Bolivian of Japanese descent who runs a restaurant mostly for Peruvian-Japanese in this industrial town some 100 km (65 miles) north of Tokyo.
The Peruvian-Japanese community in Isezaki and the surrounding area is perhaps the largest in Japan, accounting for about 4,000 of the 15,000 Peruvians in the country.

Machida's restaurant "La Bodeguita" serves as a community centre for the immigrant workers. Cans of lima beans, peppers, Peruvian beer and yellow Peruvian potatoes are sold here, and notices for year-end parties and babysitting dot the walls.

Last Friday, three days after armed Marxist guerrillas stormed into the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and took hundreds of hostages, someone threw a rock through the windshield of Machida's small van parked behind his restaurant.
On the same day, someone threw a fist-size block of concrete into a grocery store run by Peruvian-Japanese Pedro Nishimata.
"I'm really disappointed by the Japanese," Nishimata told Reuters. "I thought the Japanese were more mature."
A day earlier, Nishimata said, an old Japanese man stormed into his store and shouted: "You Peruvians are bad. You should all go back to your country."

"The police brushed the incidents off, saying it was only a minor incident. But what do you think would have happened if it was the other way around, if a Peruvian threw a rock into a Japanese shop?" Nishimata asked.
Nishimata also said a Peruvian customer had told him his boss was threatening to fire all Peruvian workers at a small welding shop.
"He said the boss wanted to replace Japanese-Peruvians with Japanese-Brazilians," Nishimata said.
The Peruvian-Japanese, like Japanese-Brazilians and other descendants of Japanese immigrants in South America, started coming to Japan in large numbers in the late 1980s, mostly as factory workers.
"Unfortunately, the hostage crisis has made us Peruvians in Japan look bad," said Nilton Ikeda, 24, a Peruvian-Japanese who works at a Sanyo plant.
Nishimata and Machida said there were no such incidents before the hostage crisis.
"I hope this ends peacefully soon," Machida said.
One middle-aged Peruvian, who came to Machida's restaurant to pick up a Christmas chicken for his family, said all countries had problems with terrorists.
"Even in a police-strong country like Japan, you had that Aum (doomsday cult) thing," said the man, who works at a plant pressing throw-away plastic lunch boxes.
"The Japanese should not think we are a nation of criminals just because of a handful of these guerrillas," the man said.
